name: def
desc: A block of code with a name, written once and used as many times as you like. Note the colon and the indent.
code:
def greet():
    print("Welcome to Data Analytics")

greet()
greet()
out:
Welcome to Data Analytics
Welcome to Data Analytics

name: Passing something in
desc: The name in the brackets is a parameter. The value you send is the argument.
code:
def greet(name):
    print("Welcome,", name)

greet("Rahul")
greet("Priya")

name: return
desc: Hands a value BACK so it can be stored or used. A function with no return hands back None.
code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

total = add(10, 20)
print(total)
print(add(5, 6) * 2)

name: print is not return
desc: The single most common confusion. print shows something; return gives it back to the code.
code:
def shows(a, b):
    print(a + b)

def gives(a, b):
    return a + b

x = shows(2, 3)
y = gives(2, 3)
print("x is", x)      # None - nothing came back
print("y is", y)

name: Returning more than one value
desc: Separate them with commas and they come back as a tuple, which you can unpack straight away.

name: 1. Positional
desc: Matched by ORDER. Swap them round and you quietly get the wrong answer, with no error.
code:
def detail(name, dept):
    print(name, "works in", dept)

detail("Rahul", "HR")
detail("HR", "Rahul")      # no error - just wrong
out:
Rahul works in HR
HR works in Rahul

name: 2. Keyword
desc: Matched by NAME, so the order stops mattering.
code:
def detail(name, dept):
    print(name, "works in", dept)

detail(name="Rahul", dept="HR")
detail(dept="HR", name="Rahul")
out:
Rahul works in HR
Rahul works in HR

name: 3. Default
desc: Give a parameter a value in the def line and it becomes optional.
code:
def detail(name, dept="Not assigned"):
    print(name, "-", dept)

detail("Rahul", "HR")
detail("Priya")              # dept falls back

name: 4. Variable length  *args
desc: One star collects any number of positional arguments into a tuple.

name: 5. Variable length  **kwargs
desc: Two stars collect any number of named arguments into a dictionary.

name: The order they must go in
desc: Positional first, then default, then *args, then **kwargs. Putting a default before a plain one is an error.
code:
def show(a, b=2, *args, **kwargs):
    print("a", a, "| b", b, "| args", args, "| kwargs", kwargs)

show(1)
show(1, 9)
show(1, 9, 100, 200, city="Chennai")

name: lambda
desc: A function with no name, written on one line. Good for something tiny you use once.
code:
double = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(21))

add = lambda a, b: a + b
print(add(10, 20))

name: map()
desc: Applies a function to EVERY item and gives back the same number of items.
code:
marks = [45, 72, 88]

out = map(lambda x: x + 5, marks)
print(list(out))

print(list(map(str, marks)))     # any function works

name: filter()
desc: Keeps only the items where the function says True. You get FEWER items back.
code:
marks = [45, 72, 88, 61, 33]

passed = filter(lambda x: x >= 60, marks)
print(list(passed))

print(list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, marks)))

name: reduce()
desc: Boils a whole list down to ONE value, two at a time. It has to be imported first.
code:
from functools import reduce

marks = [45, 72, 88]
print(reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, marks))
print(reduce(lambda a, b: a if a > b else b, marks))

name: The three side by side
desc: map keeps the count, filter reduces the count, reduce collapses it to one.
code:
from functools import reduce
m = [45, 72, 88, 61]

print("map   ", list(map(lambda x: x * 2, m)), "   same count")
print("filter", list(filter(lambda x: x > 60, m)), "      fewer")
print("reduce", reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, m), "              one")
out:
map    [90, 144, 176, 122]    same count
filter [72, 88, 61]       fewer
reduce 266               one

name: A function that calls itself
desc: Every recursion needs a base case — the condition that stops it. Without one it never ends.
code:
def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:           # base case
        print("Go")
        return
    print(n, end=" ")
    countdown(n - 1)     # calls itself

countdown(5)

name: Factorial
desc: The classic. 5! is 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1, and each step is the same problem one size smaller.

name: Fibonacci
desc: Each number is the sum of the two before it. Two base cases this time.

name: Forgetting the base case
desc: Python stops you rather than freezing — but the error is the only warning you get.
code:
import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(100)

def forever(n):
    return forever(n - 1)      # nothing stops it

forever(5)

name: The short way to build a list
desc: A for loop and an append, written on one line. Read it as: what I want, then where it comes from.
code:
# the long way
squares = []
for n in range(1, 6):
    squares.append(n * n)
print(squares)

# the same thing
squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)

name: With a condition
desc: Put the if at the END and it filters — only the items that pass get built.
code:
marks = [45, 72, 88, 61, 33]

print([m for m in marks if m >= 60])
print([m * 2 for m in marks if m % 2 == 0])

name: if ... else inside one
desc: When you want a value for EVERY item, the if-else goes at the FRONT. That trips people up.
code:
marks = [45, 72, 88, 61]

print(["pass" if m >= 60 else "fail" for m in marks])

name: On a string, and nested
desc: Anything you can loop over, you can comprehend over.
code:
print([c.upper() for c in "python"])
print([x for x in "statistics" if x in "aeiou"])
print([[i * j for j in range(1, 4)] for i in range(1, 4)])

name: Dictionary comprehension
desc: Same idea with curly brackets and a key : value pair.
code:
depts = ["HR", "Tech", "Sales"]
print({d: len(d) for d in depts})
print({n: n * n for n in range(1, 6)})
